runs.t: A photograph is only as useful as its reading.
Screening asks one question per image:
The answer rests on small signs — a few microaneurysms, a haemorrhage near the edge — and on whether the image can be read at all.
Readers disagree, and cases near a boundary are where errors cluster.

slides.notes: The problem. Diabetic retinopathy can damage sight before symptoms appear, so screening programmes photograph the retina and a reader decides: refer, or re-screen. That decision rests on small signs and on whether the image can be read at all. Two errors matter and they are not equal: a false negative sends disease home; a false positive causes an unnecessary referral. The screenshot is our viewer with the answer deliberately hidden.

runs.t: Reading accuracy can be measured — case by case.
Readings can be scored against a reference.
On a defined set, each human reading is compared with a reference label: sensitivity, specificity — and where the errors cluster.
The same protocol can test any AI aid, honestly.
Patient-level split, threshold fixed on validation data only, one test pass. No model has been evaluated yet.
Does an AI aid improve clinicians?
That needs a controlled reader study. This project makes no such claim and the app says so.

slides.notes: The research hypothesis in three parts, each tagged honestly. H1 we demonstrate educationally: a reading can be scored against a reference. H2 is specified and the statistics engine is built and unit-tested, but no model has been evaluated. H3, whether an AI aid improves clinician accuracy, is future work and needs a controlled reader study - we make no such claim.

slides.notes: Expert reference standards. We use the ICDR five-level scale (Wilkinson et al., Ophthalmology 2003). Referable means moderate NPDR or worse, or suspected macular oedema. The 4-2-1 rule defines severe disease. Important honesty point: in this prototype the reference label is authored from each case's own lesion list and re-derived by an automated test - it is a teaching reference, not an independent expert panel. A real study needs several graders and adjudication.

slides.notes: The Diagnostic Duel. The reader sees an image with no label, records an interpretation, locks it, and only then sees what the reference says. Because no model exists, the duel is Human vs Reference and is never labelled Human vs AI. The score is educational - a small synthetic set, not validated clinical performance - and it does not show that AI improves clinicians. If a reader opens the reference first, that case becomes practice-only and is excluded from the score.

slides.notes: Actual research-model evaluation. The honest answer: there is none. This machine has no Python environment, no GPU and no licensed research dataset, and training a toy model on sixteen synthetic drawings would be meaningless. So the protocol is specified in full, the statistics engine is implemented and tested, and the Laboratory will compute real results the moment a held-out predictions file is supplied. Until then every empty state says not implemented.

slides.notes: Responsible clinical integration. Before any clinical use there is a path: retrospective validation on a locally representative, patient-split dataset; silent prospective evaluation; an assisted-reading study that measures accuracy, time and automation bias; and regulated deployment with monitoring. This prototype stops before step one. Inside the prototype the safeguards are a human in the loop, a blind-first duel, five-way provenance, no fabrication, a no-result pathway, leakage control and privacy by design. The ledger on the right shows the five things we never merge.

Build a patient-level split manifest and remove near-duplicates

Fix the threshold on validation data; spend the test partition once
Only then: a controlled reader study of AI assistance
